# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

**"Other tests" means the project's suite, not just your file.** A
green run of the test you wrote is not a green suite. Before you call
the change done, run the project's test command (bare `pytest`,
`npm test`, `cargo test` — whatever the repo uses) even when your task
named only one test file. A scope statement in your task bounds the
deliverable, not your verification. Any failure that run shows —
including one you didn't cause — goes in your report by name; a red
test you watched scroll past and didn't mention is a report falsified
by omission.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

When writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:
- Name the production change that would make the test fail — before writing it
- Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior
- Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes
- Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests written after pass immediately — which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)" | Tests-after answer "what does this do?"; tests-first answer "what should this do?" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote — you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |
| "Already manually tested" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. "Worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy — that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. "Pragmatic" shortcuts mean debugging in production — slower, not faster. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

git push -q -u origin HEAD 2>&1 | tail -2; gh pr create --base main --title "feat: brain status reports hosted connection state (COR-2108)" --body "## Why

\`entire brain status\` said nothing about the hosted brain. The only signals were a blind-spot note and stderr lines from background syncs, so a user could not tell whether their repo was sharing memories, waiting to connect, or suppressed by the egress kill switch.

## What

Status (short, verbose, and \`--json\`) now reports one of three hosted states, gated in the same order as the sync path (kill switch first, then the binding):

- \`connected\` — \`hosted.json\` present; shows repo id, base URL, and the fact branches whose per-branch \`hosted-target.json\` matches the current target (stale markers from an older target do not count).
- \`local_only\` — no binding; auto-connect keeps retrying.
- \`disconnected\` — \`ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS\`/\`LOCAL_ONLY\` set; the suppressed target stays visible so the reader sees what the switch is blocking.

A corrupt \`hosted.json\` degrades to \`local_only\` with a warning instead of failing status. The JSON key is additive (\`hosted\`), and COR-2109's explicit opt-out will reuse the \`disconnected\` state.

Short-report example:
\`\`\`
  …/entire-brain | manifest current | 2447 facts | hosted: disconnected (ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS/LOCAL_ONLY set)
\`\`\`

## Validation

- New tests cover all three states, stale-marker exclusion, and the corrupt-binding warning (\`internal/cli/hosted_status_test.go\`), written before the implementation.
- \`go test ./...\` green; gofmt clean.
- Built the binary and verified all three states render against a real brain.

Ticket: [COR-2108](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2108/brain-status-show-hosted-vs-local-only-connection-state)

Now I'm weighing fixes — adding a distinct error/invalid status, treating a corrupt binding as absent so sync overwrites it, or some other status-side signal — but overwriting on read failure risks clobbering a valid binding on a transient error, and this finding is really about status honesty rather than changing sync behavior.

content.text:
# Review PR

Review a pull request with structured, actionable feedback.

## Arguments

- `363` — PR number, URL, or branch name. If empty, review the current branch's open PR.

## Process

### 1. Fetch PR context

```
gh pr view <pr> --json title,body,baseRefName,headRefName,additions,deletions,changedFiles,commits,author
gh pr diff <pr>
```

Read the PR description carefully — it defines scope and intent. Everything you review should be evaluated against what the PR is trying to accomplish.

### 2. Understand the change

Before reviewing line-by-line:
- What is this PR doing and why?
- What files are touched and what's the blast radius?
- Are there any architectural implications?

### 3. Review with this checklist

**Correctness**
- Does the code do what the PR description says?
- Are there logic errors, off-by-one bugs, or unhandled edge cases?
- Are error paths handled correctly?

**Security**
- Any injection risks (SQL, XSS, command injection)?
- Are secrets, tokens, or credentials handled safely?
- Are inputs validated at system boundaries?

**Testing**
- Are there tests for the new/changed behavior?
- Do tests cover edge cases, not just the happy path?
- Are test assertions meaningful (not just "doesn't throw")?

**Design**
- Does the change follow existing codebase patterns and conventions?
- Is the abstraction level appropriate (not over/under-engineered)?
- Are there unnecessary changes outside the stated scope?

**Performance**
- Any N+1 queries, unbounded loops, or missing pagination?
- Are there opportunities for batching or caching that were missed?
- Will this scale with the data sizes it will encounter?

**Readability**
- Are names clear and consistent with the codebase?
- Is complex logic adequately explained?
- Would a future reader understand the "why" behind non-obvious decisions?

### 4. Adversarial review

Take a second, adversarial pass over the diff. Actively try to break the change — assume it has flaws and hunt for them across:

- **Performance** — worst-case inputs, hot paths, allocations, contention.
- **Stability** — race conditions, partial failures, retries, resource leaks, crash recovery.
- **Correctness** — inputs and states that violate the author's assumptions.
- **Simplicity** — code that could be deleted or replaced with something simpler/stdlib.
- **Platform design standards** — deviations from the platform's established design patterns and conventions.

Add any findings to the output using the same severity format.

### 5. Run /simplify

Run the `/simplify` skill (via the Skill tool) against the changed code and fold its findings into the review output.

### 6. Structure your output

For each finding, use this format:

**[severity] file:line — short title**
Description of the issue and why it matters. Include a suggested fix when possible.

Severity levels:
- **[blocking]** — Must fix before merge. Correctness bugs, security issues, data loss risks.
- **[important]** — Should fix. Design problems, missing tests for critical paths, performance issues.
- **[nit]** — Nice to fix. Style, naming, minor improvements. Don't block merge on these.
- **[question]** — Not necessarily wrong, but needs clarification or discussion.

### 7. Summary

End with a brief summary:
- Overall assessment (approve / request changes / needs discussion)
- What the PR does well
- Top 1-3 items that need attention
- Any scope concerns (changes that seem unrelated to the stated goal)

## Guidelines

- Review what's in the diff, not what you wish was there. Don't request unrelated refactoring.
- If the PR is large, focus on the most impactful files first.
- Be specific — "this could be better" is not useful. Show what "better" looks like.
- Distinguish between "this is wrong" and "I would do this differently." Only the former is blocking.
- If you're unsure about something, use [question] severity instead of asserting it's wrong.
- Read relevant source files (not just the diff) when you need context about how changed code integrates with the rest of the system.

content.text:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

content.thinking:
I realize readMemoryStateFile failures can stem from real tamper signals like path-safety violations or symlink attacks, not just corruption — yet the self-heal logic treats all of these as "absent" and silently overwrites the binding, which means a tampered hosted.json would get rewritten instead of flagged.

Actually, since the atomic write replaces via temp+rename, it destroys rather than follows a symlink, so self-heal does neutralize that particular tamper vector; the bigger concern is a transient I/O error combined with an explicit staging binding getting silently clobbered toward a prod placement, which is low-probability but worth flagging as a [question] with an option to tighten self-heal to parse-errors only. I'm noting this as my first finding while waiting for the other four agents to finish.

Beyond that, I have a few smaller notes: the daemon-tick hint message is unchanged and consistent, there's trivial duplication of a corrupt-JSON test literal across two files, and the verbose render branch for local_only is a bit much and might get flagged by other reviewers. Now I'm just waiting on the agent notifications to come in.

I flagged one issue in my adversarial review: the self-heal now suppresses all binding read errors (I/O and tamper-check failures), not just corrupt JSON. I'll detail this in the final review once the four cleanup agents finish.

Pushed (`721cd2cc` — GitHub rejected the first attempt again, transient, succeeded on retry). Here's the full review:

---

## Review of PR #363 — brain status reports hosted connection state

**[fixed] `internal/cli/hosted_sync.go:40` — corrupt binding stranded the repo (Bugbot, medium)**
Status called a corrupt `hosted.json` "local_only — auto-connect will retry," but the sync path returned on the read error and never retried. Fixed in `62ab3ad0`: the read error now falls through to auto-connect, which re-resolves placement and rewrites the binding; pinned by `TestHostedSyncRepairsCorruptBinding`.

**[question] `internal/cli/hosted_sync.go:40` — the self-heal swallows every read error, not just corrupt JSON**
`readHostedRepoBinding` fails for parse errors but also for I/O and tamper-check failures (path safety, non-regular file, oversize). All now count as "absent," so a transient read failure on an explicitly configured binding (e.g. a staging target set via `connect --repo-id/--api-url`) could get silently rewritten to resolved placement — redirecting fact egress to a different cell. Low likelihood, real consequence. If you want it tighter, self-heal only on the `"invalid hosted repo binding"` parse error and keep the loud skip for I/O errors. Fine to defer to COR-2112, which reworks auto-connect consent anyway.

**[nit, skipped] gate-order duplication between `buildHostedStatus` and `hostedFactsSyncAndPull`**
The altitude reviewer suggested extracting a shared "connection gate." I skipped it: the two sites share only two reads and an env check, their shapes differ (early-return flow with side effects vs. report assembly), and the new sync test pins the contract. Extraction would be a forced abstraction at this size.

**[applied] simplify findings** — `buildHostedStatus` returned a warnings slice that could only hold one item (now a string), and the verbose state line duplicated an `Fprintf` (now one call with a suffix). Committed as `721cd2cc`. Reuse and efficiency reviews came back clean — the diff consistently reuses `readHostedRepoBinding`, `checkHostedFactsBinding`, `brainNoEgressMode`, and the warnings convention.

**Pre-existing flake, disclosed:** `TestOllamaDistillAgentEnvelopeAllowanceIsCeilinged` failed intermittently (7/30 runs) during verification — in this checkout directory only. The same commits pass 0/42 in clean worktrees and fresh subdirs, and base code shows the same profile, so it's not a regression from this PR: the test asserts a server goroutine writes ≤ ceiling+4MB while deliberately streaming to ceiling+8MB, and the margin loses to socket-buffer/scheduler jitter under local file-watcher load. Worth its own ticket if you see it in CI — say the word and I'll file it.

### Summary
**Approve.** The PR does what it says: one honest `hosted` section computed in the builder, rendered identically on all three surfaces via a shared label, additive JSON, TDD'd end to end including the corrupt-binding and stale-marker edges. The one open item is the [question] above — breadth of the self-heal — which is a deliberate-tradeoff call, not a blocker. Validation: targeted tests green, full suite green apart from the unrelated flake documented above, gofmt clean.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/evisdrenova/.claude/plugins/cache/entire-skills/entire/0.7.2/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

20	// hostedFactsSyncAndPull closes the hosted-memory loop for one branch: publish
21	// the branch's local facts through factsync.Sync (read-merge-CAS), record the

23	// authors — back into the local branch store so teammates' facts become
24	// first-class in brief/recall.

27	// a nil return, because its callers (daemon tick, session-end hook, connect)
28	// must not fail on hosted outages. The error return exists for programming
29	// errors only.

31	// Gate order is fixed: (1) the local-only kill switch always wins; (2) a
32	// recorded opt-out (`entire brain disconnect`) stops sync AND auto-connect
33	// until `connect` clears it; (3) the repo binding is the connection state —
34	// absent, each run tries to resolve it through the host CLI and falls back to
35	// local-only, silently, until that succeeds; (4) apiurl.Validate before any
36	// client exists. A fresh token is minted per call via the host CLI's own login
37	// and held only in memory.

61			// Auto-connect: placement comes from the host CLI (repo view), which
62			// fails for a logged-out user, an unregistered repo, or a CLI without

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_entire-prod-us__get_entire_trail
entries.description:
One trail in full — metadata, discussion, reviewers, and its checkpoints — with a console deep link. One call replaces the piecemeal trail REST reads.

When to use:
  - "What's the state of trail N?" — status, discussion, approvals, and linked checkpoints in one read.
  - Following a trail number from search_entire_trails or a console URL.

Addressed by the repo (prefixed path or ULID) and the trail number. Load the entire/trails skill for the trail lifecycle.

Pairs with: search_entire_trails (find the number); compare_entire_refs (trail branch vs default — the actual code delta); get_entire_session (the AI work behind trail commits).

repo.description: the repository: a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, or git/<owner>/<repo>) or a 26-char repo ULID

number.description: the trail number within the repo

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_entire-prod-us__trail_findings
entries.description: Manage a trail's code-review findings (the CLI calls the same thing `entire trail finding`; the wire type is a review comment). list shows every finding on the trail, or scope it to one review with reviewId. get/update/create address a finding by trail + finding id alone — omit reviewId on get/update and the finding's owning review is found automatically; omit it on create and a review opens implicitly, the same two-step entire-api call the CLI's `finding add` makes as one. Also covers get_review (a review's own record) and files (the file content it covers). Mutating for update/create.

repo.description: the repository: a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, or git/<owner>/<repo>) or a 26-char repo ULID

action.description: list, get, update, create, get_review, or files

reviewId.description: review id; optional for list/get/update/create (see action docs), required for get_review/files

status.description: list: CSV filter open,resolved,dismissed; update: new status (one value) — resolved/dismissed require statusReason

severity.description: list: CSV filter high,medium,low; update: new severity (one value)

cursor.description: list: opaque cursor from a prior response's next_cursor

confidence.description: update: new confidence, 0-1 (0 is a valid value, distinct from omitting the field)

statusReason.description: update: reason; required when status becomes resolved or dismissed

comments.description: create: one JSON-encoded finding object per item, in entire-api's snake_case publish schema: client_id, body, severity, confidence, status, status_reason, location {granularity (line|range|file|whole_change), file_path, start_line, end_line, start_column, end_column, selected_text, nearby_text, language}, suggested_change {change_type, patch, instruction, expected_file_path, expected_start_line, expected_end_line, expected_lines}; multiple items post a batch

summary.description: create: optional review summary; concludes the review

paths.description: files: comma-separated file paths (max 200) to fetch reviewed content for

I see the CLI list filtered out stale items, and the first one is a bug where buildHostedStatus never checks OptedOut, causing status to show connected after disconnect — but this was already fixed in commit 5ccb5d10, with the exact branch and test requested.

The other remaining items were already resolved earlier (labels, self-heal). The last one is a real, still-applicable issue: checkHostedFactsBinding conflates absent/mismatch/corrupt states for per-branch markers, so a corrupt hosted-target.json silently looks like "never synced" instead of warning. I'm weighing how to fix it cleanly — either have buildHostedStatus read and unmarshal the marker itself (duplicating logic) or refactor checkHostedFactsBinding to distinguish corrupt/read-error from absent/mismatch and surface a warning.

I'm thinking through adding a readHostedFactsBinding helper that returns the binding plus a found flag and error, mirroring the hosted.json pattern — any read error becomes warn-worthy. But this reopens a problem: buildHostedStatus currently returns a single warning string after a prior simplification, and now I need to support multiple warnings again since both top-level and per-branch issues can surface. I'm deciding whether to revert to a warnings slice or aggregate per-branch warnings into one combined line, while noting the top-level and per-branch warning cases are actually mutually exclusive since a top-level binding read failure would skip the branch loop entirely.

I'm settling on aggregating multiple corrupt branch markers into a single warning listing the affected branch names plus the first encountered error for diagnosis, keeping the return type as a single string. For testing, I plan to write a garbage JSON file as a branch's hosted marker alongside a valid binding, expecting the branch to stay out of SyncedBranches while the status still reports connected with a warning mentioning the marker issue — then I start implementing the new helper function in facts_hosted_binding.go.

content.text:
Root cause found and fixed, pushed as `e7100a99`. CI is re-running on PR #363.

**What was failing:** one test, Windows only — `TestHostedSyncSkipsUnreadableBindingWithoutRewrite` (the guard I added for the trail finding). It used `os.Chmod(binding, 0o000)` to make `hosted.json` unreadable, but on Windows that only toggles the read-only attribute — reads still succeed. So the test's "unreadable" binding parsed fine and the sync proceeded, even attempting a real DNS lookup of its fake staging host. The two other red jobs (coverage/integrity, aggregate) were downstream of that shard.

**Fix:** the test now puts a *directory* at the binding path — that fails the read with a non-parse error on every platform — and asserts the skip happens without re-resolution and the path is left untouched. The production self-heal gate is unchanged; this was purely test portability.

Also in this push:
- The corrupt branch-marker fix from the last trail finding (`bb6136c7`), now committed.
- Rebased over two more main merges that landed on the branch meanwhile (COR-2114 watch-tick sync; no conflicts, hosted tests green after).

Worth knowing: the only unreadable-binding trigger that works cross-platform is shape-based (directory), not permission-based — if the Windows runner surfaces more of these, that's the pattern to reach for.

content.thinking:
I'm finding two issues: a high-severity one where a corrupt binding file combined with a prior opt-out causes the self-heal logic to silently bypass the privacy opt-out and resume syncing—a real privacy violation—and a medium-severity one where the verbose local_only message inaccurately suggests auto-reconnection will happen.

The user's pushback is fair: all these cascading edge cases trace back to a single decision I made—adding self-heal logic for corrupt bindings during the sync path that wasn't part of the original ticket. The simpler fix is to remove the self-heal entirely: treat a corrupt binding as a loud, consistent failure, update the status message to not promise auto-connect, and let the user manually run the connect command that now exists. The original Bugbot complaint was really about the status wording being misleading, not about sync behavior—so the fix belongs on the status side, not by making sync handle corruption automatically.

Both findings resolved on trail 279, fix pushed as `c2695d2b`.

And you're right — I was overcomplicating it. The status feature itself was always just read-and-print. The complexity came from one bad call I made along the way: having the *background sync* self-heal a corrupt binding file (added to satisfy the first review finding). That one behavior kept spawning real edge cases — custom targets, then the high finding: a corrupt file could hide a recorded `disconnect`, and the self-heal would silently reconnect and resume publishing past the user's privacy opt-out, because it couldn't re-read the opt-out from the very file it was healing.

The fix is deletion, not another patch:

- **Sync:** any unreadable `hosted.json` → one stderr line, skip, never rewrite. Auto-connect runs only when the file is truly absent. The sentinel error and its special case are gone — the diff is net-negative.
- **Status (the high finding's sibling):** the local-only line now says `not connected; run 'entire brain connect' to join` — true for both "no binding" and "unreadable binding" — instead of promising an auto-connect that sync won't do; the unreadable-binding warning names the same remedy.

Both changes were test-first (`TestHostedSyncSkipsCorruptBindingWithoutReconnect` pins the privacy rule; the status test asserts no auto-connect promise), full suite green except the known dir-local Ollama flake, and I recorded the rule in Brain so no future session re-adds a self-heal: **never rewrite a binding you can't read — the only remedy is explicit `connect`.**

content.text:
Mostly no — it's stale now. That finding made three claims; here's each against the current code:

1. **"Status says auto-connect will retry, but sync never resolves a corrupt binding"** — no longer accurate. The auto-connect promise is gone from every surface: verbose local-only now says `not connected; run 'entire brain connect' to join` and the warning says `hosted binding unreadable (run 'entire brain connect' to rebind): …`. Both statements are true for a corrupt binding — sync deliberately skips it (the self-heal came and went in between; the final behavior is skip, by the privacy rule from the trail's high finding).

2. **"Corrupt binding renders as the same state as a missing binding"** — still true, but now by design rather than by accident. Both are `local_only`, distinguished by the warning; and since the remedy (`connect`) and the rendered text are correct for both cases, the shared state no longer misleads anyone.

3. **"The short line hides it, so a stuck binding looks like a healthy wait"** — softened. The short report's health line flips from `healthy` to `… 1 warning` whenever the binding is unreadable (`buildStatusHealth` counts `report.Warnings`), so short mode does signal something's wrong; the warning *text* appears in `--verbose` and `--json`. A corrupt binding also no longer means "stuck" — nothing waits on it, the fix is one explicit command.

The GitHub comment is also anchored to `hosted_status.go:74`, which has shifted several commits since. Bugbot should mark it outdated on its next pass; if it doesn't, it's safe to resolve the thread manually with a pointer to `c2695d2b`.

content.text:
The plugin symlinks to a binary at your main checkout (`~/conductor/repos/entire-brain/entire-brain`), so rebuild there first:

```bash
# 1. Rebuild the installed plugin from merged main
cd ~/conductor/repos/entire-brain
git checkout main && git pull origin main
go build -o entire-brain ./cmd/entire-brain
```

Then, from any Entire-enabled repo (this one works):

```bash
# 2. Baseline — expect "… | Local-only" on the identity line
entire brain status
entire brain status --verbose     # → Local-only (run 'entire brain connect' to join Brainstore)

# 3. Connect — expect "connected: …", then "Connected to Brainstore"
entire brain connect              # needs login + registered repo; if placement
                                  # can't resolve (cli#2758 not in your CLI yet):
                                  # entire brain connect --repo-id <ulid> --api-url https://<cell>
entire brain status               # → … | Connected to Brainstore
entire brain status --verbose     # → Connected to Brainstore (N branches synced / no branches synced yet)

# 4. Disconnect — expect the opt-out wording, not the kill switch
entire brain disconnect
entire brain status --verbose     # → Disconnected from Brainstore (run 'entire brain connect' to rejoin)

# 5. Kill switch — expect the env var named exactly as set
ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS=1 entire brain status --verbose   # → Disconnected from Brainstore (ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS set)
ENTIRE_BRAIN_LOCAL_ONLY=1 entire brain status --verbose  # → … (ENTIRE_BRAIN_LOCAL_ONLY set)

# 6. Corrupt binding — expect Local-only + a warning, and NO auto-reconnect
B=~/.local/share/entire/plugins/data/brain/repos/gh/entireio/entire-brain
cp "$B/hosted.json" /tmp/hosted.json.bak   # if it exists
echo '{not json' > "$B/hosted.json"
entire brain status --verbose     # → Local-only (…) plus Warnings: hosted binding unreadable (run 'entire brain connect' to rebind)
entire brain connect              # the one sanctioned repair
# or restore: cp /tmp/hosted.json.bak "$B/hosted.json"

# 7. Machine contract — full detail lives only here
entire brain status --json | jq .hosted
# → {"state":"connected","repo_id":"…","base_url":"…","synced_branches":[…]}
```

Two things to watch: step 3's plain `connect` resolves through `entire repo view --json`, so it only auto-resolves once cli#2758 is in your installed CLI — the `--repo-id/--api-url` flags are the workaround until then. And in step 6, confirm no background tick "fixes" the corrupt file on its own — it must stay broken until you run `connect`; that's the privacy guarantee from the trail's high finding.

content.text:
Two answers first, then I'll do both tasks:

**What those things are:** `manifest: current` means the brain's on-disk index manifest matches the schema this binary supports (other values: `stale`, `absent` — i.e., "is this store readable as-is"). The **semantic index** is the code-structure index (symbols, relations) that powers `query`/`inspect code`; you don't have one because it's built by `entire brain refresh --agent none` and that's never been run to completion on this store — that's also why status nags about it.

**Why slow:** what the evidence shows — 30s user + 35s *system* time at 86% CPU means it's burning local compute and syscalls, not waiting on network. Status does real work per call: the facts integrity cross-check re-reads every branch's fact store (30 branches), plus live-state git calls and the sessions/exchange projections. Which one dominates needs profiling — that's the ticket, I won't guess further.

COR-2109 connect/disconnect DONE 2026-10-14 (entire-brain PRs #364/#369/#370): `entire brain disconnect` writes opted_out:true into hosted.json keeping coordinates (not a purge — pulled teammate memories stay local); auto-connect writes via bindHostedRepoIfNotOptedOut (re-checks opt-out under the brain write lock, closing the disconnect-during-resolution race); placement resolution switched whereami→`entire repo view --json` (top-level repoId/apiUrl) — DORMANT until entireio/cli#2758 merges (flagless connect falls back to stored coordinates meanwhile); banners render via shared renderHostedBanner (blank line + bold headline + left-aligned dim paragraphs). Merge/closed-trail visibility and teammate distribution are all DERIVED from reachability — no promote events (v2's hole: branch heads without promote meant teammates on main never received merged facts locally), no recycle markers, lineage.json cancelled. content.thinking:
I'm comparing the two: 2113 just needs verification and is blocked on the nightly CLI build landing in about 1.5 hours, so it's low effort with no design work left. 2112 is heavier — it involves the consent model and has an external dependency on a contract change to carry the org opt-in signal, plus plugin-side work, so it needs more coordination before it can move.

My recommendation is to verify 2113 first since it's quick and unblocks auto-connect going live, but start 2112's contract work in parallel immediately because it's the longer pole — if 2113 ships live without 2112's consent gating, every registered repo gets silent auto-connect, which is exactly the privacy gap Evis wanted closed by choosing option (c).

There's real urgency here: brainstore is live on four prod cells, so once auto-connect flips on, it means real publishing for real users, not a hypothetical. The opt-in signal needs to live across two repos — a CLI ticket for the repo-view piece and an API ticket for the server-side enablement flag — so I should draft the contract (field name, semantics) and file both tickets, keeping the response focused on the recommendation, rationale, and concrete next steps rather than diving into the work itself since they just wanted to talk it through.

content.text:
Both — but they're different kinds of "next," and the order matters for a privacy reason.

**2113 is next chronologically, and it's ~an hour.** The code is on main; the next nightly (~06:30 UTC) is the first CLI that can run it. Install, run `entire brain connect` flagless, confirm a fresh clone auto-binds on a daemon tick. That's the whole ticket.

**2112 should start now, in parallel, because 2113 going live *creates* the problem 2112 exists to fix.** The moment people run a CLI with #2758, auto-connect wakes up with the implicit consent model: logged in + repo registered = facts start publishing on the next session-end, silently. Brainstore is live on four prod cells, so that's real egress for real users, not staging. You decided against exactly that (option c: org enablement counts as consent, auto-connect only maintains it). Right now nothing enforces it.

2112 is also the long pole, because it's cross-repo:

1. **Contract** — the placement surface (`repo view --json` or whatever backs it) must carry a "hosted brain enabled for this repo" signal, not just coordinates. That's an entireio/cli + entire-api change that needs its own tickets and an owner; nobody has started it.
2. **Plugin side** — auto-connect requires the signal, loud first-sync notice, opt-out precedence (that last part already shipped with disconnect). This part is small once the contract exists.

So the practical sequencing: verify 2113 when the nightly drops and close it — but treat **CLI release adoption as the clock on 2112**. The safety margin is how slowly users upgrade, not anything in the code. If that margin feels too thin, there's a stopgap worth considering: a one-line plugin change that keeps auto-connect dormant behind a flag until 2112 lands, shippable today.

Want me to draft the contract (field name + semantics) and file the cli/api tickets for 2112, and/or the stopgap?

Ultimately I decide to just run the real flagless connect test since the repo's already connected and the rewrite/sync is idempotent anyway. I need to make sure the plugin picks up the newly built CLI, so I'll set up a PATH override pointing to a symlinked binary so `entire brain connect` dispatches through the new build rather than the old installed one.

After running it I'll mark 2113 verified and move on to designing 2112 — presenting the contract and plugin fail-closed behavior in chat, then figuring out where org-level hosted-brain enablement should live server-side, which touches the entire-api catalog work.

Since the user wants to proceed with 2112, I'll sketch a concrete proposal: the CLI's `repo view --json` output gets a top-level `brainSyncEnabled` flag that's only true when the org has explicitly enabled hosted brain sync for that repo, with the server carrying this through placement/catalog data and the CLI passing it along like it does repoId and apiUrl — fail-closed on both sides. On the plugin side, I can build this now by adding a `BrainSyncEnabled` field to the hosted placement struct and wiring the auto-connect logic to respect it, while filing CLI/API tickets separately once the contract design gets approved.

Auto-connect should bind only if the resolved placement signals BrainSyncEnabled; otherwise it stays local silently and retries later. But explicit `entire brain connect` runs should work regardless of that signal — since the user is deliberately invoking the command, that itself counts as traceable consent, so the org-level flag should only gate automatic binding, not explicit connect. I also want a one-time loud notice when auto-connect first binds, printed to stderr noting the repo now syncs to the org's hosted brain and how to disconnect — though I'm aware that visibility is weak in background/daemon contexts, so the notice may need to surface elsewhere too.

Opt-out precedence already shipped, so I'll treat verification as covering both the contract check and the flagless connect e2e test. {"id":"COR-2112","uuid":"8fb6fc3d-3c90-490d-8314-d31519d74510","title":"Consent model: explicit opt-in per repo; auto-connect only maintains it","description":"**Decision (Evis, 2026-10-13):** hosted sync requires explicit opt-in per repo. Org-level enablement (the admin registering the repo for hosted brain) counts as the opt-in. Auto-connect only *maintains* an existing opt-in — e.g. a fresh clone of a repo the org enabled — it never creates consent by itself.

Today the opposite is true: when the daemon tick or session-end hook finds no binding and host-CLI placement resolution succeeds (user logged in + repo registered), the repo silently starts publishing facts (`internal/cli/hosted_sync.go:44-58`). The user never said yes and gets no output.

**Required**

* Auto-connect binds only when the resolved placement carries the org-level opt-in signal (needs a contract change in the placement surface — now `entire repo view --json` (`repoId`/`apiUrl`, <pull-request id="3556a88b-1d77-4764-a8c7-2e3aa1608ddb" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/review/feat-expose-hosted-repo-coordinates-in-repo-view-json-bf3a5a210dbd">entireio/cli#2758</pull-request>) — to say "hosted brain enabled for this repo", not just "repo exists").
* Without that signal, nothing syncs until the user runs `entire brain connect`.
* Loud first-sync notice either way: one clear line saying this repo now syncs memories to <org>'s hosted brain, and how to disconnect.
* Explicit `disconnect` state wins over any auto-connect (see connect/disconnect ticket).
* `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS` / `LOCAL_ONLY` remains the absolute kill switch above all of this.

content.text:
COR-2113 closed (verification comment attached), COR-2112 In Progress. Here's the 2112 design — sign off and I'll build the plugin side today.

## Contract (cross-repo, needs cli + api tickets)

`repo view --json` gains one top-level field: **`brainSyncEnabled: true`** — present and true only when the org has enabled hosted brain for this repo. Omitted or false means not enabled. Server side: entire-api's placement/catalog carries the flag; cli passes it through exactly like `repoId`/`apiUrl`. Fail-closed at every hop.

## Plugin side (mergeable immediately, before the contract ships)

1. `hostedPlacement` gains `BrainSyncEnabled bool`. **Auto-connect binds only when it's true.** Today's CLI never emits the field → auto-connect goes dormant the moment this merges, which is exactly the safety property we want while the contract is being built. When cli/api ship the field, auto-connect wakes up only for enabled repos.
2. **Explicit `entire brain connect` ignores the signal** — a human running the command *is* the consent, traceable to a person. Flags path unchanged too. (This also keeps the team unblocked right now: this repo stays connectable regardless.)
3. **Loud first-bind notice:** auto-connect currently binds silently; it will print one line — `connected to Brainstore for <repo> (run 'entire brain disconnect' to stop syncing)` — on the trigger's stderr, and the connected state already shows in status.
4. Opt-out precedence and the kill switch are already shipped and untouched.

**Files:** `connect_cmd.go` (field), `hosted_sync.go` (gate + notice), tests for: no field → no bind; field true → binds with notice; field false → no bind; explicit connect still works without the field.

**Plus two tickets I'd file:** entireio/cli — pass `brainSyncEnabled` through `repo view --json`; entire-api — expose org/repo hosted-brain enablement in the placement data (needs an owner who knows where enablement state should live server-side; today `ENTIRE_BRAIN_HOSTED_ENABLED` is a cell-level deploy flag, not per-repo).

One consequence to be explicit about: between this merging and the contract shipping, **fresh clones won't auto-connect at all** — teammates get hosted sync via explicit `connect` only. That's the deliberate trade (dormant beats unconsented), but say so if you'd rather sequence differently.

I should clarify that by "cross-repo" I meant the change spans entireio/cli and entire-api, not just entire-brain. And on the second point, they're right to push back — repo view is a CLI/repo-placement surface, so brainSyncEnabled doesn't belong there architecturally since brain is a separate concern.

Stepping back to the actual problem: auto-connect currently treats "placement resolves" (logged in + repo registered) as permission to start publishing the team's memories to the hosted store, but registration with Entire isn't the same as consent to hosted brain sync. We need a brain-owned signal — something auto-connect can check that's traceable to an actual decision — rather than inferring consent from CLI state. One option is having the plugin probe a brainstore endpoint directly, using a 403 vs 200 response as the authorization signal rather than relying on repo view fields.

Another approach: server-side repo-level enablement, where the first explicit `connect` by a team member turns on hosted brain for the repo (making consent traceable to that person), and auto-connect for everyone else simply checks whether the server already has brain data for that repo — no new server surface needed beyond checking for existing state.

The check needs to happen before any publish: look for an existing head/fact set first; if nothing exists, the repo was never explicitly connected, so auto-connect should stay local rather than silently creating hosted data. If something exists, a teammate already consented, so auto-connect can safely join — and the upcoming per-fact redesign would make this "does any data exist" check trivial.

I should present both this lazy auto-detect approach and the server-flag alternative so they can choose, but keep my answer short and address their two direct questions first.

content.text:
Fair pushback. Let me answer both and restate the problem from zero.

**1. "Cross-repo"** just meant: my proposal needed changes in three codebases — entireio/cli (pass the field through), entire-api (store/serve the enablement bit), and entire-brain (check it). That's the cost you're rightly questioning.

**2. You're right about the struct.** `repo view` answers "where does this repo live" — a placement question. "Does this repo sync memories" is a brain question, and leaking it into the CLI's repo status couples two domains for no reason. Dropping that idea.

**The actual problem, stated plainly:** auto-connect fires when placement resolves — meaning *"user is logged in and the repo is registered with Entire."* But registering a repo with Entire is not consent to publish the team's memories to a shared store. Those are different decisions, and today the code treats the first as the second. We need auto-connect to ask "did someone on this team actually opt this repo into hosted brain?" before it publishes anything.

And once it's phrased that way, there's a signal that already exists, brain-owned, with no new contract anywhere: **the hosted store itself.** If a teammate ever ran `entire brain connect` and published, the repo has brain data server-side. So:

- **Explicit `connect` creates consent** — a person ran a command; traceable. (Already works.)
- **Auto-connect asks brainstore "does this repo have any brain data?"** — a GET against the endpoint the plugin already authenticates to. Data exists → a teammate opted in → bind and join. No data → nobody ever consented → stay local, retry later, publish nothing.

That is literally your recorded decision — "auto-connect only maintains an existing opt-in, never creates it" — implemented as one read-before-bind in `hosted_sync.go`. No cli change, no api change, no new field, no admin toggle to build. The only wrinkle: today's read endpoint is per-branch (`GET facts?branch=`), so "any data?" means checking the default branch first — imperfect until COR-2123's repo-wide `facts?since=` feed lands, at which point the check becomes exact for free.

Want me to build it that way?

func newSetupCommand(opts Options) *cobra.Command {
	setupOpts := defaultSetupOptions()
	cmd := &cobra.Command{
		Use:   "setup [path]",
		Short: "Build the brain and start background updates",
		Long: fmt.Sprintf(`setup is the one command that makes a repository's brain useful and keeps it
that way. It runs three phases:

  1. instant   build the deterministic core (semantic index, sessions, seed,
               docs, history). Blocking, seconds, spends NO agent tokens. The
               brain is queryable the moment this returns.
  2. backfill  distill past sessions into durable facts, NEWEST FIRST, detached
               in the background on a cheap model. Spends tokens; bounded by
               --backfill-budget and the persisted distill cache, and skipped
               entirely when no agent CLI is available.
  3. daemon    register the repo into a workspace and install ONE machine-wide
               watcher service (launchd on macOS, a systemd user unit on Linux)
               so freshness never depends on remembering to run anything.
               ONE means one: the installed unit is identical for every repo and
               every workspace, and each workspace's interval, distill cadence,
               agent, model, effort and session cap live in a machine-level watch
               plan the running watcher re-reads. Setting up a second repo adds a
               row to that plan; it does not rewrite, restart or steal the
               watcher the first repo is relying on.

TOKEN SPEND: phases 2 and 3 call an agent. This is the first release in which
the watcher's --distill step and the session-end hook's distill actually run
(both were dead before), so setup is a real, recurring cost, bounded by four
gates: --backfill-budget sessions per background pass, one gated agent run per
--distill-every per repo, the persisted distill cache (a session is never
distilled twice), and the cheap --model/--effort. Passing --no-backfill with
--no-daemon spends nothing at all, and "%[1]s status" reports what the
backfill has done so far and whether the watcher is alive.

EXIT CODE: setup exits 0 whenever the brain is queryable — that is, whenever at
least one instant-phase component built. A component that fails (a semantic
index whose snapshot carries a different repo key, say) is reported as one line,
skipped, and the remaining components, the backfill, the workspace registration
and the daemon install all still run; "%[1]s status" then shows that
component as failed and "%[1]s doctor" prints the reason. setup exits
non-zero only when nothing usable exists: the brain directory cannot be built,
or every component failed.

Re-running setup is safe: it detects the existing workspace membership and
daemon instead of duplicating them, resumes rather than restarts a backfill
that is still running, and keeps whatever --interval/--distill-every/--model/
--effort the previous run was given unless you pass the flag again.`, setupCommandPrefix(os.LookupEnv)),
		Args: cobra.MaximumNArgs(1),
		RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
			return runSetup(cmd.Context(), cmd, opts, setupOpts, agentSurfaceTarget(opts, args), setupSteps{})
		},
	}
	cmd.Flags().StringVar(&setupOpts.workspace, "workspace", setupOpts.workspace, "Workspace the repo joins (created when absent)")

content.text:
Setup is non-interactive (three phases, no prompts), so here's the bounded design:

**Delete auto-connect.** `hostedFactsSyncAndPull` with no binding → silent local-only return, every time. The only ways a binding comes to exist:
1. `entire brain connect` (flagless now works, or `--repo-id/--api-url`),
2. **onboarding:** `entire brain setup --connect` — new flag that runs the same bind + first sync as the connect command at the end of setup. Without the flag, setup's completion output prints one hint line: `memories stay local — run 'entire brain connect' to sync with your team`. No interactive prompt (setup has none today, and daemons re-run it).

**Consequences, stated plainly:**
- A fresh clone never syncs until that person runs `connect` (or `setup --connect`) themselves — per-machine opt-in, since `hosted.json` is per-machine state. "Auto-connect maintains an existing opt-in" is gone entirely; the opt-in *is* the binding on disk.
- `disconnect` keeps working as the off switch; re-running `setup` won't resurrect a connection (opt-out marker still wins, and there's no auto path left anyway).
- Status wording already matches (`local-only — run 'entire brain connect' to join Brainstore`); no changes there.
- Dead code falls out: the auto-connect block in `hosted_sync.go`, `bindHostedRepoIfNotOptedOut`'s race guard (connect is now always foreground), and the auto-connect tests get inverted to "no binding → zero requests, no bind, silent."
- COR-2112's description gets rewritten to this decision (the old option-c "org enablement counts as consent" is superseded — consent is now always a person running a command on their machine), and I'll update the Brain facts to match.

Files: `hosted_sync.go`, `setup.go` (flag + hint), `connect_cmd.go`/`hosted_binding.go` (dead-code removal), tests.

Good to build?

8	// brainStatusHosted is the status report's hosted-brain connection section.
9	// States: "connected" (repo binding present), "local_only" (no binding; only
10	// `entire brain connect` creates one), "disconnected" (the egress kill switch is set;
11	// COR-2109 adds the explicit opt-out as a second cause of this state).
12	type brainStatusHosted struct {
13		State   string `json:"state"`
14		RepoID  string `json:"repo_id,omitempty"`
15		BaseURL string `json:"base_url,omitempty"`
16		// SyncedBranches are the declared fact branches whose per-branch marker
17		// matches the current binding; a marker left by an older target does not
18		// count.
19		SyncedBranches []string `json:"synced_branches,omitempty"`
20	}
21	
22	const (
23		hostedStateConnected    = "connected"
24		hostedStateLocalOnly    = "local_only"
25		hostedStateDisconnected = "disconnected"
26	)
27	
28	// buildHostedStatus reports this repo's hosted connection state with the same
29	// gate order as hostedFactsSyncAndPull: the kill switch wins, then the binding
30	// decides. The binding stays visible under the kill switch so the reader sees
31	// what it suppresses. A corrupt binding degrades to local_only with a warning
32	// rather than failing status over a sync-state file.
33	func buildHostedStatus(brainDir string, factBranches []string) (*brainStatusHosted, string) {
34		var warning string
35		hosted := &brainStatusHosted{State: hostedStateLocalOnly}
36		binding, present, err := readHostedRepoBinding(brainDir)
37		switch {
38		case err != nil:
39			warning = "hosted binding unreadable (run 'entire brain connect' to rebind): " + err.Error()
40		case present && binding.OptedOut:
41			// Coordinates survive an opt-out (reconnect needs no placement
42			// resolution), so the target stays visible here too.
43			hosted.State = hostedStateDisconnected
44			hosted.RepoID = binding.RepoID
45			hosted.BaseURL = binding.BaseURL
46		case present:
47			hosted.State = hostedStateConnected
48			hosted.RepoID = binding.RepoID
49			hosted.BaseURL = binding.BaseURL
50			// A broken marker is corruption, not "never synced" — report it like
51			// the unreadable top-level binding above instead of posing as a
52			// healthy unsynced branch. The two warnings cannot co-occur: markers
53			// are only inspected when the binding itself was readable.
54			var broken []string
55			var brokenErr error
56			for _, branch := range factBranches {
57				marker, markerPresent, markerErr := readHostedFactsBinding(brainDir, branch)
58				switch {
59				case markerErr != nil:
60					broken = append(broken, branch)
61					if brokenErr == nil {
62						brokenErr = markerErr
63					}
64				case markerPresent && marker.RepoID == binding.RepoID && marker.BaseURL == binding.BaseURL:
65					hosted.SyncedBranches = append(hosted.SyncedBranches, branch)
66				}
67			}
68			if len(broken) > 0 {
69				warning = fmt.Sprintf("hosted sync marker unreadable for branch(es) %s: %v", strings.Join(broken, ", "), brokenErr)
70			}
71		}
72		if brainNoEgressMode() {
73			hosted.State = hostedStateDisconnected
74		}
75		return hosted, warning
76	}
77	
78	// hostedStateLabel is the short-report value for the "Brainstore:" item; the
79	// cause and remedy live in the verbose line (hostedStatusLine).
80	func hostedStateLabel(state string) string {
81		switch state {
82		case hostedStateConnected:
83			return "connected"
84		case hostedStateDisconnected:
85			return "disconnected"
86		default:
87			return "local-only"
88		}
89	}
90	
91	// hostedStatusLine is the verbose report's one-line hosted state: the label
92	// plus the cause or remedy. Coordinates are machine detail and stay in --json.
93	func hostedStatusLine(h *brainStatusHosted) string {
94		switch h.State {
95		case hostedStateConnected:
96			if n := len(h.SyncedBranches); n > 0 {
97				word := "branches"
98				if n == 1 {
99					word = "branch"
100				}
101				return fmt.Sprintf("Connected to Brainstore (%d %s synced)", n, word)
102			}
103			return "Connected to Brainstore (no branches synced yet)"
104		case hostedStateDisconnected:
105			// Two causes share the state and the kill switch wins the gate order,
106			// so it also wins the blame line. Name the variable actually set.
107			switch {
108			case securityToggleEnabled("ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS"):
109				return "Disconnected from Brainstore (ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS set)"
110			case securityToggleEnabled("ENTIRE_BRAIN_LOCAL_ONLY"):
111				return "Disconnected from Brainstore (ENTIRE_BRAIN_LOCAL_ONLY set)"
112			default:
113				return "Disconnected from Brainstore (run 'entire brain connect' to rejoin)"
114			}
115		default:
116			return "Local-only (run 'entire brain connect' to join Brainstore)"
117		}
118	}

patch.old_string: **Decision (Evis, 2026-10-13):** hosted sync requires explicit opt-in per repo. Org-level enablement (the admin registering the repo for hosted brain) counts as the opt-in. Auto-connect only *maintains* an existing opt-in — e.g. a fresh clone of a repo the org enabled — it never creates consent by itself.
patch.new_string: **Decision (Evis, 2026-10-15, supersedes 2026-10-13):** by default a repository has NO connection to the hosted brain. The only two ways to connect are `entire brain connect` and the onboarding flow (to be built). Auto-connect is removed entirely — background triggers never create a connection. The binding on disk is both the consent record and the connection state. Earlier option (c) (org enablement counts as consent, auto-connect maintains it) and the placement-signal contract change are superseded; no cli/api changes needed.

* Explicit `disconnect` state wins over any auto-connect (see connect/disconnect ticket).
* `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS` / `LOCAL_ONLY` remains the absolute kill switch above all of this.

content.text:
COR-2112 is built and up for review — **[PR #379](https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/379)**.

**What it does:** a repo never connects to the hosted brain by default. `hostedFactsSyncAndPull` with no binding is a silent local-only no-op on every trigger; the only opt-ins are `entire brain connect` (and the onboarding flow when you build it — I left a hook for that: setup's closing *Next* block now offers `entire brain connect — sync memories with your team (off by default)` on unbound repos, and stays quiet for connected or opted-out ones). Auto-connect is deleted outright, which also removes `bindHostedRepoIfNotOptedOut` and the disconnect-during-resolution race — net code got simpler, not bigger.

**Validation:** core test written first and watched fail (resolvable placement + valid token + no binding → zero requests, no binding written, silent); setup golden updated; three obsolete auto-connect tests deleted; full suite green except the known dir-local Ollama flake.

**Bookkeeping:** COR-2112 retitled ("Hosted sync is opt-in only: no remote connection by default") with the superseding decision and implemented list; the Brain fact records the reversal chain (2026-10-07 "connect automatically" → 2026-10-13 option c → 2026-10-15 default-off) so no future session resurrects auto-connect.

One operational note: machines that already have a `hosted.json` (like yours, from testing) keep syncing — the binding is grandfathered as consent, which is correct since connect wrote it. Fresh clones and new machines start local-only until someone runs `connect`. The trail review will pass over it shortly; point me at any findings.
